And why will the answer need the absolute value of x, often read as mod x?

Think about what a primitive means here. We want a curve whose gradient, at each x, equals the height of one over x. For positive x, we already know one. The derivative of the natural log of x is one over x. At x equals two, the log curve has gradient one half, the same as the height of one over x at two. But one over x has a second piece on the left, where x is negative. The natural log of x doesn't exist there, so it can't be the whole answer.

On the left, one over x is negative, so the curve we want must go downhill as x increases. Near zero it must be steep, and further left it must flatten out. That's the log curve, mirrored in the y axis. Mirroring left to right reverses every slope. At x equals minus two, the mirrored curve has gradient minus one half, and one over minus two is minus a half. This mirrored curve is the natural log of minus x. The chain rule confirms it. Its derivative is one over minus x, times the inner derivative, minus one. That's one over x.

Put the two pieces together. For positive x we have the natural log of x, and for negative x, the natural log of minus x. Both are the natural log of mod x. Mod x is the size of x without its sign. Now watch the gradient as a point moves along each piece. On both sides, it traces one over x exactly. So the integral of one over x is the natural log of mod x, plus C, for x not equal to zero.

Notice the gap at zero. One over x isn't defined there, and mod x doesn't fill the gap. So this primitive is two separate pieces. Slide the right piece up, and its gradients don't change. Slide the left piece down, and the same is true. Nothing joins the pieces across zero, so each one can have its own constant. Differentiate any of these curves, and you get one over x on each piece. Here's the pattern to remember. When the top is the derivative of the bottom, the answer is the natural log of mod bottom. If the top is a constant multiple of that derivative, fix the number in front. And keep the absolute value, unless the bottom is always positive.
